items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries”.
items.answer: Drainage basin
items.markingKey: Drainage basin: the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries. [1]

items.stem: Explain how vegetation affects the amount of water reaching a river.
items.answer: Vegetation intercepts rain and slows it; roots help infiltration and plants take up water and transpire it, so less water reaches the river and more slowly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark interception; 1 mark infiltration/transpiration [2]

items.stem: Explain why the lag time is shorter in an urban drainage basin than in a forested one.
items.answer: Impermeable surfaces and drains carry water quickly to the river with little infiltration; in forest, interception and infiltration slow the water down.
items.markingKey: 1 mark impermeable/drains; 1 mark contrast with forest [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 is a storm hydrograph for the River Ock. Rainfall peaked at 12 mm per hour at 14:00 on day 1. Discharge rose from a base flow of 8 cumecs to a peak of 48 cumecs at 08:00 on day 2. Suggest two reasons why the lag time may be long.
items.answer: Gentle slopes; permeable rock and soil allowing infiltration; dense forest intercepting rain; large or elongated basin; dry soil before the storm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 is a storm hydrograph for the Mekong. Rainfall peaked at 18 mm per hour at 09:00 on day 1. Discharge rose from a base flow of 20 cumecs to a peak of 90 cumecs at 15:00 on day 1. (a) Calculate the lag time. (b) Explain why the falling limb is less steep than the rising limb.
items.answer: (a) 6 hours (b) After rainfall stops, water continues to reach the river slowly by throughflow and groundwater flow, so discharge falls gradually.
items.markingKey: (a) 15:00 on day 1 − 09:00 day 1 = 6 h [1] (b) 1 mark slower flows; 1 mark gradual fall [2]

items.stem: Freya argues that human activity has a greater effect than physical factors on the shape of a storm hydrograph. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: deforestation; rock type.
items.answer: For: Urbanisation adds impermeable surfaces and drains, shortening lag time and raising peak discharge. Deforestation removes interception; farming practices compact soil. Against: Rock type, slope, basin shape, soil saturation and rainfall intensity control run-off speed in all basins. In remote upland basins physical factors dominate. Judgement: In urban basins human factors often dominate; elsewhere physical factors such as rainfall intensity and geology are usually more important.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: A student writes: “When soil is already saturated, more rain will soak into it.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Saturated soil cannot absorb more water, so rain becomes surface run-off and flood risk rises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “erosion caused by the force of water hitting the bed and banks and forcing air into cracks”.
items.answer: Hydraulic action
items.markingKey: Hydraulic action: erosion caused by the force of water hitting the bed and banks and forcing air into cracks. [1]

items.stem: Explain why rivers erode most during floods.
items.answer: Velocity and discharge are higher, so the river has more energy; it carries more and larger load, increasing abrasion and hydraulic action.
items.markingKey: 1 mark more energy/velocity; 1 mark more load and erosion [2]

items.stem: Explain why the load of a river becomes smaller and more rounded downstream.
items.answer: Attrition knocks stones together and abrasion wears them, breaking off edges over a long distance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark attrition; 1 mark over distance/time [2]

items.stem: Students measured the River Tees at Site 1, near the source. Width = 4.5 m, mean depth = 0.5 m. A float took 25 s to travel 5 m. (a) Calculate the velocity in m/s. (b) Suggest one way of making the velocity measurement more reliable.
items.answer: (a) 0.2 m/s (b) Repeat the float timing three times and take the mean; use a flow meter; avoid windy conditions.

items.stem: Students measured the River Tees at Site 1, near the source. Width = 12 m, mean depth = 0.5 m. A float took 16 s to travel 5 m. (a) Suggest why surface float velocity may be higher than the mean velocity. (b) Suggest one way of making the velocity measurement more reliable.
items.answer: (a) Friction with the bed and banks slows water near them, so surface water in mid-channel flows fastest. (b) Repeat the float timing three times and take the mean; use a flow meter; avoid windy conditions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark friction; 1 mark surface fastest [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Students measured the River Severn at Site 5, near the confluence. Width = 6 m, mean depth = 0.5 m. A float took 10 s to travel 5 m. (a) Calculate the velocity in m/s. (b) Suggest why surface float velocity may be higher than the mean velocity. (c) Suggest one way of making the velocity measurement more reliable.
items.answer: (a) 0.5 m/s (b) Friction with the bed and banks slows water near them, so surface water in mid-channel flows fastest. (c) Repeat the float timing three times and take the mean; use a flow meter; avoid windy conditions.
items.markingKey: (a) 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 m/s [1] (b) 1 mark friction; 1 mark surface fastest [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that erosion is the most important river process in shaping river landscapes? Use examples you have studied. You may wish to consider: lower course; floods; upper course.
items.answer: For: Vertical erosion forms V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and gorges; lateral erosion forms meanders and wide valleys. Against: Deposition builds flood plains, levees, deltas and slip-off slopes in the lower course. Transportation links them: load carried from upstream drives abrasion. Judgement: Erosion dominates in the upper course and deposition in the lower course; the landscape is the result of all three processes working together.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows measurements at five sites downstream along a river. Site 1 (0 km from source): width 1.6 m, mean pebble size 183 mm. Site 2 (4 km from source): width 2 m, mean pebble size 133 mm. Site 3 (9 km from source): width 4.6 m, mean pebble size 91 mm. Site 4 (15 km from source): width 6.8 m, mean pebble size 17 mm. Site 5 (22 km from source): width 7.1 m, mean pebble size 69 mm. Describe how channel width changes downstream. Use data.
items.answer: Width increases from 1.6 m at Site 1 to 7.1 m at Site 5.
items.markingKey: 1 mark trend; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a steep drop in a river’s course where water falls over a band of hard rock lying on top of softer rock”.
items.answer: Waterfall
items.markingKey: Waterfall: a steep drop in a river’s course where water falls over a band of hard rock lying on top of softer rock. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a waterfall and gorge form.
items.answer: Hard rock lies over soft rock; the soft rock is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion, undercutting the hard rock to leave an overhang; the overhang collapses into the plunge pool; repeated collapse makes the waterfall retreat upstream, leaving a gorge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rock bands; 1 mark undercut/overhang; 1 mark collapse; 1 mark retreat/gorge [4]

items.stem: Explain how an ox-bow lake forms.
items.answer: Erosion on the outside of meander bends narrows the meander neck; during a flood the river cuts through the neck and takes the shorter, straighter course; deposition seals off the old bend, leaving an ox-bow lake.
items.markingKey: 1 mark erosion of outer bends; 1 mark neck cut in flood; 1 mark deposition seals [3]

items.stem: Fig. 3.2 is a sketch of a river in its middle course. The river forms a large bend. On the outside of the bend is a steep bank 3 m high with exposed tree roots; on the inside is a gently sloping bank of sand and gravel. Further downstream, a narrow neck of land separates two bends that are only 40 m apart. Name the landforms on the outside and inside of the bend.
items.answer: Outside: river cliff. Inside: slip-off slope.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 3.2, a sketch map of a meandering river. A steep, eroding bank lies on the outside of one bend and a gently sloping beach of sand and gravel on the inside. Downstream, two meander loops almost meet across a narrow neck of land. (a) Name the landforms on the outside and inside of the bend. (b) Explain the difference between the two banks.
items.answer: (a) Outside: river cliff. Inside: slip-off slope. (b) Water is deeper and faster on the outside, so lateral erosion (hydraulic action, abrasion) undercuts the bank; on the inside water is slow and shallow, so sediment is deposited.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark outside; 1 mark inside [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 3.2, a sketch map of a meandering river. A steep, eroding bank lies on the outside of one bend and a gently sloping beach of sand and gravel on the inside. Downstream, two meander loops almost meet across a narrow neck of land. (a) Name the landforms on the outside and inside of the bend. (b) Draw and describe a cross-section from the river cliff to the slip-off slope.
items.answer: (a) Outside: river cliff. Inside: slip-off slope. (b) Steep cliff on one side, deepest water close to it, channel becoming shallow towards the gently sloping deposits on the other side (asymmetrical).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark asymmetry; 1 mark labels [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.3 shows a waterfall in the upper course of a river. The river flows over a band of hard sandstone 8 m thick lying on top of soft shale. There is an overhang of sandstone above a deep plunge pool. Downstream is a narrow steep-sided gorge 250 m long. (a) Explain how the overhang has formed. (b) Explain how the gorge has formed.
items.answer: (a) Soft rock beneath is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion (splashback), undercutting the hard rock. (b) The overhang collapses repeatedly and the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a steep-sided gorge.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark differential erosion; 1 mark undercutting [2] (b) 1 mark collapse; 1 mark retreat [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.2 is a sketch of a river in its middle course. The river forms a large bend. On the outside of the bend is a steep bank 3 m high with exposed tree roots; on the inside is a gently sloping bank of sand and gravel. Further downstream, a narrow neck of land separates two bends that are only 40 m apart. (a) Explain what is likely to happen to the narrow neck of land in the future. (b) Draw and describe a cross-section from the river cliff to the slip-off slope.
items.answer: (a) Erosion on the outside bends will narrow the neck further; in a flood the river will cut through, forming a straight channel and later an ox-bow lake. (b) Steep cliff on one side, deepest water close to it, channel becoming shallow towards the gently sloping deposits on the other side (asymmetrical).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark erosion narrows; 1 mark cut-off in flood; 1 mark ox-bow [3] (b) 1 mark asymmetry; 1 mark labels [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Meanders stay in the same place for hundreds of years.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Erosion on the outside and deposition on the inside make meanders migrate across and down the flood plain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “when a river overflows its banks and covers land that is normally dry”.
items.answer: Flood
items.markingKey: Flood: when a river overflows its banks and covers land that is normally dry. [1]

items.stem: Explain how deforestation upstream can increase flooding downstream.
items.answer: With fewer trees, less rain is intercepted and transpired, and soil is eroded into the river, reducing channel capacity; more water reaches the river faster.
items.markingKey: 1 mark less interception; 1 mark faster run-off; 1 mark sediment reduces capacity [3]

items.stem: Explain why river flooding is both a hazard and a benefit to people living on flood plains.
items.answer: Hazard: destroys homes, crops and roads, causes deaths and disease. Benefit: deposits fertile alluvium, provides water for crops and fish.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hazard; 1 mark benefit [2]

items.stem: Study your case study of a river flood (for example the Pakistan floods, 2022). Briefly explain the causes of the flood.
items.answer: the Pakistan floods, 2022: Exceptionally heavy monsoon rains from June to August (about three times the 30-year average in August), on top of a heatwave that increased glacial melt in the Himalayas and Karakoram; the Indus and its tributaries overflowed; poor drainage and deforestation added to the problem.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Physical causes (rainfall intensity/duration, snowmelt, saturated soil, relief) and human causes (deforestation, urbanisation), linked to the named river. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of a river flood (for example the Pakistan floods, 2022). Briefly describe the responses to the flood.
items.answer: the Pakistan floods, 2022: Government and army rescue; UN appeal; international aid for food, tents and medical care; rebuilding of homes and embankments; debate about climate finance for vulnerable countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Short-term rescue and aid; long-term management and planning. [4]

items.stem: For a named example of a river flood that you have studied, describe the responses to the flood.
items.answer: Model answer (flooding in Bangladesh, 1998): Emergency food aid and boats; later the Flood Action Plan: embankments, cyclone and flood shelters on raised platforms, improved warnings and raised houses.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Short-term rescue and aid; long-term management and planning. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: A river near Toronto has a bankfull discharge of 140 cumecs. Table 3.2 shows daily rainfall and mean river discharge. day 1: 70 mm, 61 cumecs. day 2: 55 mm, 142 cumecs. day 3: 18 mm, 139 cumecs. day 4: 18 mm, 150 cumecs. day 5: 0 mm, 120 cumecs. What was the total rainfall?
items.answer: 161 mm

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “building artificial structures, such as dams, embankments and relief channels, to control rivers”.
items.answer: Hard engineering
items.markingKey: Hard engineering: building artificial structures, such as dams, embankments and relief channels, to control rivers. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a dam and reservoir reduce flood risk.
items.answer: The reservoir stores water during heavy rain and releases it slowly, controlling discharge downstream.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stores water; 1 mark controlled release [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of building embankments.
items.answer: Advantage: increase channel capacity so water stays in the channel. Disadvantage: expensive, may fail catastrophically, stop fertile silt reaching fields and move flooding downstream.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Study your case study of a river management scheme (for example flood management in Bangladesh). Briefly describe the methods used to manage the river.
items.answer: flood management in Bangladesh: The Flood Action Plan built embankments along major rivers, raised flood shelters and houses on earth platforms, and improved flood warnings sent by radio and mobile phone; soft measures include floating gardens and community training.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named structures/techniques with dimensions, dates, costs; how each reduces flood risk. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of a river management scheme (for example the Jubilee River flood relief channel, UK). Briefly evaluate the success of the scheme.
items.answer: the Jubilee River flood relief channel, UK: It protects about 3000 properties and created wildlife habitats; however, during the 2014 floods it was blamed for increasing flooding in villages downstream, and it was expensive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Advantages and disadvantages for people, the economy and the environment, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: For a named example of a river management scheme that you have studied, describe the methods used to manage the river.
items.answer: Model answer (the Three Gorges Dam, Yangtze River, China): A 2.3 km-wide, 185 m-high concrete dam completed in 2006 (fully operational 2012) with a 600 km-long reservoir; stores floodwater to protect millions downstream; 32 turbines generate up to 22.5 GW of hydro-electric power; ship locks improve navigation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Named structures/techniques with dimensions, dates, costs; how each reduces flood risk. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: For a named example of a river management scheme that you have studied, evaluate the success of the scheme.
items.answer: Model answer (flood management in Bangladesh): Shelters and warnings have cut deaths sharply, but embankments are costly to maintain, can fail and stop fertile silt reaching fields; the scale of flooding means management reduces impacts rather than stopping floods.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Advantages and disadvantages for people, the economy and the environment, with a judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the boundary of a drainage basin, usually a ridge of high land”.
items.answer: Watershed
items.markingKey: Watershed: the boundary of a drainage basin, usually a ridge of high land. [1]

items.stem: Explain how steep slopes and impermeable rock affect a storm hydrograph.
items.answer: Water cannot soak into impermeable rock and flows quickly down steep slopes as surface run-off, so the peak discharge is higher and the lag time shorter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark faster run-off; 1 mark higher peak/shorter lag [2]

items.stem: In one year a drainage basin receives 1800 mm of precipitation. Evapotranspiration is 540 mm and river run-off is 750 mm. The rest is added to storage (soil water and groundwater). Suggest how the figures would differ in a hot, forested basin.
items.answer: Evapotranspiration would be a larger share because of high temperatures and transpiration by trees; less run-off.
items.markingKey: 1 mark more evapotranspiration; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: “Human activity has a greater effect than physical factors on the shape of a storm hydrograph.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: urbanisation; deforestation.
items.answer: For: Urbanisation adds impermeable surfaces and drains, shortening lag time and raising peak discharge. Deforestation removes interception; farming practices compact soil. Against: Rock type, slope, basin shape, soil saturation and rainfall intensity control run-off speed in all basins. In remote upland basins physical factors dominate. Judgement: In urban basins human factors often dominate; elsewhere physical factors such as rainfall intensity and geology are usually more important.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “erosion when rocks carried by the river scrape and wear away the bed and banks”.
items.answer: Abrasion
items.markingKey: Abrasion: erosion when rocks carried by the river scrape and wear away the bed and banks. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a river deposits its load on the inside of a meander bend.
items.answer: Water is shallower and slower on the inside bend, so it loses energy and drops sand and gravel, forming a slip-off slope.
items.markingKey: 1 mark slower velocity; 1 mark deposition/slip-off slope [2]

items.stem: Students measured the Rhine at Site 1, near the source. Width = 12 m, mean depth = 0.25 m. A float took 16 s to travel 5 m. Suggest why surface float velocity may be higher than the mean velocity.
items.answer: Friction with the bed and banks slows water near them, so surface water in mid-channel flows fastest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark friction; 1 mark surface fastest [2]

items.stem: Students measured the Rhine at Site 3, in the middle course. Width = 3 m, mean depth = 0.4 m. A float took 25 s to travel 5 m. (a) Calculate the discharge. Show your working and give units. (b) Suggest one way of making the velocity measurement more reliable.
items.answer: (a) 0.24 m³/s (cumecs) (b) Repeat the float timing three times and take the mean; use a flow meter; avoid windy conditions.
items.markingKey: (a) discharge = area × velocity = 1.2 × 0.2 = 0.24 cumecs [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that erosion is the most important river process in shaping river landscapes? Use examples you have studied. You may wish to consider: landforms; upper course; floods.
items.answer: For: Vertical erosion forms V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and gorges; lateral erosion forms meanders and wide valleys. Against: Deposition builds flood plains, levees, deltas and slip-off slopes in the lower course. Transportation links them: load carried from upstream drives abrasion. Judgement: Erosion dominates in the upper course and deposition in the lower course; the landscape is the result of all three processes working together.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “waterfall”?
options: A deep pool at the foot of a waterfall eroded by hydraulic action and abrasion.
A steep drop in a river’s course where water falls over a band of hard rock lying on top of softer rock.
A narrow, steep-sided valley formed as a waterfall retreats upstream.
Ridges of higher land that the river winds around in the upper course.
items.answer: A steep drop in a river’s course where water falls over a band of hard rock lying on top of softer rock.
items.markingKey: Waterfall: a steep drop in a river’s course where water falls over a band of hard rock lying on top of softer rock. [1]

items.stem: Explain how levees are formed.
items.answer: When the river floods it loses velocity as it spreads over the flood plain; the largest, heaviest sediment is deposited first next to the channel; repeated floods build up raised banks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark loss of velocity; 1 mark coarse material first; 1 mark repeated floods [3]

items.stem: Fig. 3.3 shows a waterfall in the upper course of a river. The river flows over a band of hard sandstone 8 m thick lying on top of soft shale. There is an overhang of sandstone above a deep plunge pool. Downstream is a narrow steep-sided gorge 250 m long. Suggest why this landform is found in the upper course rather than the lower course.
items.answer: Steep gradient, vertical erosion and outcrops of hard and soft rock are typical of upland areas.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Deposition is more important than erosion in forming the landforms of the lower course of a river.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: flood plains; deltas.
items.answer: For: Levees, flood plains, deltas and slip-off slopes are all depositional. Against: Meanders and ox-bow lakes need lateral erosion on outer bends. River cliffs are erosional. Judgement: Deposition is dominant in the lower course, but many lower-course landforms result from erosion and deposition acting together.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Study Fig. 3.3, a diagram of a waterfall. A layer of resistant rock caps a softer rock below. The water falls 20 m into a plunge pool; an overhang has formed at the lip. Below the falls the river flows through a gorge. (a) Describe how the plunge pool forms. (b) Suggest why this landform is found in the upper course rather than the lower course.
items.answer: (a) Falling water and swirling boulders erode the bed by hydraulic action and abrasion, deepening a pool. (b) Steep gradient, vertical erosion and outcrops of hard and soft rock are typical of upland areas.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Floods are always caused by heavy rainfall alone.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Snowmelt, saturated ground, impermeable rock, deforestation, urbanisation and storm surges can all contribute.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why the impacts of floods are often greater in LICs than HICs.
items.answer: Dense populations on flood plains, poorly built homes, few defences, weak warning systems and less money for rescue and insurance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: A river near Bangkok has a bankfull discharge of 140 cumecs. Table 3.2 shows daily rainfall and mean river discharge. day 1: 70 mm, 80 cumecs. day 2: 2 mm, 67 cumecs. day 3: 55 mm, 155 cumecs. day 4: 5 mm, 131 cumecs. day 5: 42 mm, 156 cumecs. day 6: 55 mm, 197 cumecs. day 7: 12 mm, 178 cumecs. Suggest two human actions that could increase the flood risk in this drainage basin.
items.answer: Building on the flood plain (impermeable surfaces, drains); deforestation upstream; draining wetlands; overgrazing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Hard engineering always stops floods completely.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Structures are designed for floods of a certain size and can be overtopped or fail, as levees did in New Orleans in 2005.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A town in a river valley near Bogotá must choose a flood scheme. Table 3.3: Option 1: straighten and deepen the channel – cost $12 million, protects 1200 properties. Option 2: raise and extend embankments (levees) – cost $20 million, protects 500 properties. Option 3: plant trees in the upper basin (afforestation) – cost $1.5 million, protects 400 properties. Calculate the cost per property protected for each option.
items.answer: Option 1: $10,000; Option 2: $40,000; Option 3: $3750
items.markingKey: cost ÷ properties for each (1 mark for two correct, 2 for three) [2]

items.stem: A town in a river valley near Lima must choose a flood scheme. Table 3.3: Option 1: raise and extend embankments (levees) – cost $30 million, protects 200 properties. Option 2: build a dam and reservoir upstream – cost $20 million, protects 1200 properties. Option 3: plant trees in the upper basin (afforestation) – cost $2 million, protects 600 properties. (a) Calculate the cost per property protected for each option. (b) Identify which options are hard engineering and which are soft engineering.
items.answer: (a) Option 1: $150,000; Option 2: $16,667; Option 3: $3333 (b) Option 1: hard; Option 2: hard; Option 3: soft
items.markingKey: (a) cost ÷ properties for each (1 mark for two correct, 2 for three) [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a smaller river or stream that joins a larger river”.
items.answer: Tributary
items.markingKey: Tributary: a smaller river or stream that joins a larger river. [1]

items.stem: Describe the shape of a storm hydrograph and explain the rising limb.
items.answer: Base flow, then a steep rising limb to peak discharge, then a gentler falling limb; the rising limb shows run-off and throughflow reaching the river after rain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shape; 1 mark rising limb explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 is a storm hydrograph for the River Ock. Rainfall peaked at 25 mm per hour at 09:00 on day 1. Discharge rose from a base flow of 15 cumecs to a peak of 30 cumecs at 19:00 on day 1. Suggest two reasons why the lag time may be long.
items.answer: Gentle slopes; permeable rock and soil allowing infiltration; dense forest intercepting rain; large or elongated basin; dry soil before the storm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.1 is a storm hydrograph for the Rhine. Rainfall peaked at 18 mm per hour at 10:00 on day 1. Discharge rose from a base flow of 10 cumecs to a peak of 30 cumecs at 18:00 on day 1. (a) Calculate the increase in discharge from base flow to peak. (b) Suggest two reasons why the lag time may be short. (c) Explain why the falling limb is less steep than the rising limb. (d) Describe how the hydrograph would change if the basin were urbanised.
items.answer: (a) 20 cumecs (b) Steep slopes; impermeable rock or saturated soil; urban surfaces and drains; small, circular basin; little vegetation. (c) After rainfall stops, water continues to reach the river slowly by throughflow and groundwater flow, so discharge falls gradually. (d) Shorter lag time, higher and steeper peak, because impermeable surfaces and drains speed up run-off.
items.markingKey: (a) 30 − 10 = 20 cumecs [1] (b) 1 mark each reason [2] (c) 1 mark slower flows; 1 mark gradual fall [2] (d) 1 mark change; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “erosion when rocks carried by the river knock into each other, becoming smaller and rounder”.
items.answer: Attrition
items.markingKey: Attrition: erosion when rocks carried by the river knock into each other, becoming smaller and rounder. [1]

items.stem: Compare traction and saltation.
items.answer: Both move load along the bed; traction rolls the largest boulders, saltation bounces smaller pebbles and sand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows measurements at five sites downstream along a river. Site 1 (0 km from source): width 2.7 m, mean pebble size 118 mm. Site 2 (4 km from source): width 5.2 m, mean pebble size 73 mm. Site 3 (9 km from source): width 6.3 m, mean pebble size 51 mm. Site 4 (15 km from source): width 6.5 m, mean pebble size 42 mm. Site 5 (22 km from source): width 7.4 m, mean pebble size 41 mm. Describe how pebble size changes downstream.
items.answer: Pebble size generally decreases from 118 mm to 41 mm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark trend; 1 mark data/anomaly [2]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows measurements at five sites downstream along a river. Site 1 (0 km from source): width 4.4 m, mean pebble size 207 mm. Site 2 (4 km from source): width 6.4 m, mean pebble size 194 mm. Site 3 (9 km from source): width 7.7 m, mean pebble size 66 mm. Site 4 (15 km from source): width 8.5 m, mean pebble size 131 mm. Site 5 (22 km from source): width 8.9 m, mean pebble size 28 mm. (a) Explain why pebble size changes downstream. (b) Calculate the mean pebble size for the five sites.
items.answer: (a) Attrition and abrasion break pebbles into smaller, rounder pieces as they are transported further. (b) 125.2 mm
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark process; 1 mark distance/time [2] (b) 207+194+66+131+28 = 626; ÷ 5 = 125.2 mm [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that erosion is the most important river process in shaping river landscapes. You may wish to consider: lower course; floods.
items.answer: For: Vertical erosion forms V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and gorges; lateral erosion forms meanders and wide valleys. Against: Deposition builds flood plains, levees, deltas and slip-off slopes in the lower course. Transportation links them: load carried from upstream drives abrasion. Judgement: Erosion dominates in the upper course and deposition in the lower course; the landscape is the result of all three processes working together.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “plunge pool”?
options: A narrow, steep-sided valley formed as a waterfall retreats upstream.
A bend in a river formed by lateral erosion on the outside and deposition on the inside.
Ridges of higher land that the river winds around in the upper course.
A deep pool at the foot of a waterfall eroded by hydraulic action and abrasion.
items.answer: A deep pool at the foot of a waterfall eroded by hydraulic action and abrasion.
items.markingKey: Plunge pool: a deep pool at the foot of a waterfall eroded by hydraulic action and abrasion. [1]

items.stem: A classmate claims: “Ox-bow lakes are found in the upper course of a river.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They form from meanders, which are found in the middle and lower course on flatter land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 3.2 is a sketch of a river in its middle course. The river forms a large bend. On the outside of the bend is a steep bank 3 m high with exposed tree roots; on the inside is a gently sloping bank of sand and gravel. Further downstream, a narrow neck of land separates two bends that are only 40 m apart. Draw and describe a cross-section from the river cliff to the slip-off slope.
items.answer: Steep cliff on one side, deepest water close to it, channel becoming shallow towards the gently sloping deposits on the other side (asymmetrical).
items.markingKey: 1 mark asymmetry; 1 mark labels [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 3.2, a sketch map of a meandering river. A steep, eroding bank lies on the outside of one bend and a gently sloping beach of sand and gravel on the inside. Downstream, two meander loops almost meet across a narrow neck of land. (a) Name the landforms on the outside and inside of the bend. (b) Explain what is likely to happen to the narrow neck of land in the future. (c) Draw and describe a cross-section from the river cliff to the slip-off slope.
items.answer: (a) Outside: river cliff. Inside: slip-off slope. (b) Erosion on the outside bends will narrow the neck further; in a flood the river will cut through, forming a straight channel and later an ox-bow lake. (c) Steep cliff on one side, deepest water close to it, channel becoming shallow towards the gently sloping deposits on the other side (asymmetrical).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark erosion narrows; 1 mark cut-off in flood; 1 mark ox-bow [3] (c) 1 mark asymmetry; 1 mark labels [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 3.3, a diagram of a waterfall. A layer of resistant rock caps a softer rock below. The water falls 20 m into a plunge pool; an overhang has formed at the lip. Below the falls the river flows through a gorge. (a) Describe how the plunge pool forms. (b) Explain how the gorge has formed.
items.answer: (a) Falling water and swirling boulders erode the bed by hydraulic action and abrasion, deepening a pool. (b) The overhang collapses repeatedly and the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a steep-sided gorge.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark collapse; 1 mark retreat [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Floods can bring benefits as well as problems.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They deposit fertile silt and recharge groundwater; Egyptian farming depended on Nile floods for thousands of years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe three opportunities rivers offer to people.
items.answer: Water supply for homes, industry and irrigation; fertile flood plains for farming; transport routes and trade; hydro-electric power; fishing; tourism and recreation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: A river near Dhaka has a bankfull discharge of 90 cumecs. Table 3.2 shows daily rainfall and mean river discharge. day 1: 0 mm, 30 cumecs. day 2: 55 mm, 116 cumecs. day 3: 0 mm, 93 cumecs. day 4: 30 mm, 137 cumecs. day 5: 70 mm, 202 cumecs. Explain why the discharge does not fall to zero on dry days.
items.answer: Base flow is maintained by groundwater and throughflow reaching the river slowly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark base flow; 1 mark groundwater/throughflow [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Flood warnings do not stop floods but can reduce their impacts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They give time to move people, valuables and vehicles to safety.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A town in a river valley near Seoul must choose a flood scheme. Table 3.3: Option 1: build a flood relief channel – cost $5 million, protects 400 properties. Option 2: install a flood warning system – cost $2 million, protects 100 properties. Option 3: straighten and deepen the channel – cost $8 million, protects 1200 properties. Which option gives the best value for money? Use your answer to support your choice.
items.answer: Option 3 (straighten and deepen the channel), lowest cost per property ($6667).
items.markingKey: 1 mark choice; 1 mark use of data [2]

items.stem: For the Three Gorges Dam, Yangtze River, China or another example of a river management scheme, briefly describe the methods used to manage the river.
items.answer: the Three Gorges Dam, Yangtze River, China: A 2.3 km-wide, 185 m-high concrete dam completed in 2006 (fully operational 2012) with a 600 km-long reservoir; stores floodwater to protect millions downstream; 32 turbines generate up to 22.5 GW of hydro-electric power; ship locks improve navigation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named structures/techniques with dimensions, dates, costs; how each reduces flood risk. [4]
